Empirical Research Plan: “Do Larger Police Forces Reduce Crime?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Two–stage least squares (2SLS) panel Instrumental-Variable (IV) design that exploits the staggered timing of mayoral and gubernatorial elections as instruments for annual growth in police officers per capita.

Why IV and not simple DiD?
•  The treatment is continuous (growth rate of officers per capita), not a binary policy adoption, so standard DiD is ill-suited.  
•  Police staffing decisions are endogenous to expected crime; the election calendar provides plausibly exogenous shocks to hiring that are strong (relevance) and arguably unrelated to short-run crime conditions (exclusion).  
•  The staggered elections across 59 cities and 23 years supply within-city, over-time variation while allowing city and year fixed effects to soak up confounders.

Basic model  

Second stage  
Δ ln(Crimeict) = β · Δ ln(Policepcict)  + Xʹict θ + μi + τt + εict  

First stage  
Δ ln(Policepcict) = π1 ElectionMayorict + π2 ElectionGovernorict + π3 Lag1_Electionict + π4 Lag2_Electionict + Xʹict κ + μi + τt + υict  

where Δ denotes year-to-year growth rates (or log differences) and μi and τt are city and year fixed effects.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
•  Δ ln(Police per capita)ict – the log change (≈ growth rate) in sworn officers per 1,000 residents in city i, year t, crime category c.

Instrument(s)  
•  ElectionMayorict – 1 if city i holds a mayoral election in year t, 0 otherwise.  
•  ElectionGovernorict – 1 if the state containing city i holds a gubernatorial election in year t, 0 otherwise.  
•  One- and two-year lags of each election dummy capture pre-election ramp-ups.

Control (counterfactual) observations  
•  The same city in years without the relevant election(s) forms the implicit control; city fixed effects ensure comparisons are within-city.

Treatment timing  
•  “Event” is the calendar year in which an election is held. Because staffing decisions (budget approvals, academy lead time) precede or coincide with elections, we instrument growth in police in year t with election dummies for t, t–1, and t–2.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance – Elections materially raise police hiring.  
   Plausible: Politicians have incentives to bolster visible public-safety inputs before voters decide.

A2. Exclusion – Conditional on fixed effects and controls, mayoral/gubernatorial election timing affects current crime only through its impact on police staffing, not via other channels.  
   Plausibility: Elections are scheduled exogenously, but incumbents could also change other policies (street lighting, social programs). We mitigate by controlling for state & local spending and testing for direct election effects on crime when police is omitted.

A3. No anticipatory crime shocks aligned with the electoral calendar.  
   Plausibility: It is hard to imagine criminals timing activities to mayoral cycles; we can test for pre-trends (event-study leads).

A4. Monotonicity – Elections do not cause some cities to reduce police while causing others to increase.  
   Reasonable: Hiring typically moves in the same (non-negative) direction in response to election incentives.

A5. SUTVA & no cross-city spillovers that differentially align with elections.  
   Plausibility: Violent and property crime displacement across the 59 large, geographically dispersed cities is limited; we cluster standard errors by city to account for any residual dependence.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Simultaneous election-year changes in other crime-relevant policies (e.g., social spending, sentencing).  
   Fix: Include controls for state & local welfare, education, and criminal-justice spending; add city-specific linear trends; show election-year coefficients on crime vanish once police growth is instrumented.

T2. Measurement error in police counts (Census vs police department reports).  
   Fix: Use growth rates (differences dampen level mis-measurement); instrumenting also attenuates classical measurement error bias.

T3. Serial correlation / staggered adoption issues.  
   Fix: Use city-clustered (or state-clustered) robust SEs; include year FE; run placebo tests with leads of elections to confirm no pre-trend.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)      # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)          # fast FE and IV estimation
library(readr)           # CSV import
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)  # robust se for checks

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load and prepare data
# ------------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("city_panel_1970_1992.csv")   # hypothetical filename

# Ensure year is numeric
dt[, year := as.integer(year)]

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Growth rates (Δln)
vars <- c("police_pc", "murder_pc", "rape_pc", "robbery_pc",
          "agg_assault_pc", "burglary_pc", "larceny_pc", "mv_theft_pc")

for(v in vars){
  newv <- paste0("dln_", v)
  dt[, (newv) := log(get(v)) - shift(log(get(v))), by = city_id]
}

# Election dummies and lags
setorder(dt, city_id, year)
dt[, elect_mayor  := as.integer(mayor_election == 1)]
dt[, elect_gov    := as.integer(gov_election   == 1)]
# 1-yr and 2-yr lags
dt[, `:=`(lag1_mayor = shift(elect_mayor, 1),
          lag2_mayor = shift(elect_mayor, 2),
          lag1_gov   = shift(elect_gov, 1),
          lag2_gov   = shift(elect_gov, 2)), by = city_id]

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main 2SLS: Example for violent crime total
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Create violent crime growth (sum of categories)
dt[, violent_crime_pc := murder_pc + rape_pc + robbery_pc + agg_assault_pc]
dt[, dln_violent := log(violent_crime_pc) - shift(log(violent_crime_pc)), by = city_id]

# Instruments vector
iv_vars <- ~ elect_mayor + elect_gov + lag1_mayor + lag2_mayor +
             lag1_gov + lag2_gov

# Controls: region FE, city-size FE, state/MSA spending controls (assume already)
fe_controls <- "| city_id + year"

# 2SLS
iv_formula <- as.formula(paste0("dln_violent ~ dln_police_pc + ", 
                                paste(c("state_edu_spend","state_welfare_spend",
                                        "msa_unemp_rate","msa_income"), collapse=" + "),
                                fe_controls, " | ",
                                paste(attr(terms(iv_vars), "term.labels"), collapse=" + "),
                                fe_controls))

est_iv <- feols(iv_formula, data = dt, cluster = ~city_id)
summary(est_iv)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness Check: Placebo Leads of Elections
# ------------------------------------------------------------
dt[, lead1_mayor := shift(elect_mayor, -1), by = city_id]
dt[, lead1_gov   := shift(elect_gov, -1),   by = city_id]

iv_placebo <- feols(dln_violent ~ dln_police_pc + 
                    state_edu_spend + state_welfare_spend + msa_unemp_rate + msa_income |
                    elect_mayor + elect_gov + lag1_mayor + lag2_mayor +
                    lag1_gov + lag2_gov + lead1_mayor + lead1_gov |
                    city_id + year,
                    data = dt, cluster = ~city_id)
summary(iv_placebo)
# Insignificant coefficients on the leads would support exclusion.

```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory (Becker 1968) predicts that higher probability of apprehension deters crime, so β̂ < 0 for both violent and property crime. Prior empirical work suggests elasticities around –0.3 to –0.5. I expect:

•  Violent crime elasticity ≈ –0.35 (a 10 % rise in officers per capita lowers violent crime by ~3.5 %).  
•  Property crime elasticity slightly smaller in magnitude (≈ –0.25).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV Design)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance (F-stat > 10) ........................... 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction believable after controls ............. 0.5  
C3: No manipulation of instrument timing ........................ 1  
C4: Monotonic treatment response (no “defiers”) ................. 1  
C5: No interference / spillovers across units ................... 0.5  
Total (out of 5) ................................................ 4.0

Overall, the election-calendar IV strategy combined with rich fixed effects provides a credible design to estimate the causal impact of police force size on crime.
